candidateRows: Claims that sacred books originate with a supernatural creator are unsupported, divisive, dangerous, and obstruct a rational response to religious extremism.
This establishes Harris's central case against supernatural textual authority and connects that epistemic objection to severe real-world consequences.
At the opening of the substantive exchange, Harris identifies supernatural authorship of sacred texts as the core dogma he opposes and relates it to conflict involving Islam and American religiosity.
Religious Americans are better than secular Americans at recognizing Islamic totalitarianism, so religiosity should not be treated as one undifferentiated danger.
The move supplies Prager's principal consequential defense of religious moral judgment by claiming superior recognition of the era's greatest evil.
Harris's claim that domestic religiosity and Islamic religion jointly perpetuate a dangerous religious dynamic.
Prager distinguishes American Jewish and Christian religiosity from Islamic totalitarianism and invokes Harris's prior concession about who more readily recognizes the threat.
Religious conservatives recognize Islamic extremism partly because they understand belief in divine books, but those same metaphysical premises make jihadist violence internally rational.
This converts Prager's claimed advantage for believers into support for Harris's thesis that unsupported religious premises can rationally generate catastrophic conduct.
Prager's contention that religious Americans' recognition of Islamic totalitarianism vindicates their moral outlook over secularism.
Harris concedes the observational point but argues that familiarity with divine-book belief explains it, then traces martyrdom and jihad premises to violent action.
The practical test of a worldview is its capacity to produce a good society, and the secular intellectual world has repeatedly failed to acknowledge major evils.
This articulates Prager's governing criterion for the debate and grounds his case in an alleged historical pattern of secular failure toward communism and Islamism.
Harris's emphasis on factual evidence and his implication that religious causal claims lack evidentiary support.
Prager says evidence for religion and the production of a good world are separate questions, then charges anti-religious secular institutions with moral blindness.
Atheism did not cause the atrocities of totalitarian regimes; unjustified political or religious dogma is the common danger, while open-ended rational inquiry can recover sound moral rules.
The move states Harris's general epistemic alternative to religious authority and directly rebuts the historical claim that secular disbelief explains totalitarian evil.
Prager's claim that secular liberals missed communism and other great evils while religious Americans diagnosed them correctly.

After disputing the attribution of communist and Nazi crimes to atheism, Harris broadens the objection to dogma generally and argues that moral wisdom remains discoverable through rational discussion.
The existence and apparent design of persons and the universe make an intentional creator intellectually more plausible than the view that everything arose coincidentally.
This supplies Prager's affirmative epistemic basis for belief in a creator rather than relying solely on the claimed social utility of religious morality.
Harris's challenge to justify belief that God authored moral commands rather than treating the attribution as unsupported.
When asked why he believes divine moral authorship, Prager appeals to the existence of the world and human conversation as evidence favoring creation and design.
The prohibition on murder endures because it rests on divine authority, whereas relying on human discussion requires an irrationally optimistic view of human nature.
The move directly presents the pro side's foundational claim that stable moral knowledge requires authority beyond fallible human beings and their deliberation.
Harris's position that people can discover the wisdom of prohibiting murder through open-ended rational conversation.
Following the dispute over biblical rules, Prager returns to murder as the decisive example and contrasts divine grounding with confidence in discussion and human nature.
Secular morality is grounded in the happiness and suffering of conscious creatures, whose differing capacities provide rational grounds for distinguishing human, animal, and embryonic interests.
This is Harris's affirmative ethical theory, explaining how secular reasoning can make morally relevant distinctions without appealing to sacred status or divine creation.
Prager's challenge that without belief in humanity's creation in God's image, secular ethics cannot privilege human life over animal life.
In response to examples involving chickens, unconscious humans, embryos, and fetuses, Harris grounds moral concern in possible experience, suffering, relationships, and neurological capacity.
Faith-based certainty that a fully formed soul exists at conception polarizes abortion debate and prevents nuanced secular discussion of the genuine ethical differences across development.
The move applies Harris's general anti-dogmatism case to a contested moral issue where he argues sacred premises obstruct careful ethical discrimination and public reasoning.
Prager's challenge that secular opposition to a partial-birth-abortion ban conflicts with Harris's recognition of fetal pain and viability.
Harris explains secular reluctance to discuss abortion gradations as a reaction to an entrenched religious premise that treats conception as morally conclusive.
Ethical realism is distinct from pragmatism: moral questions have right and wrong answers based on the happiness and suffering available to conscious physical systems.
This sharply formulates the con side's metaethical foundation and shows how it can criticize dogmatic errors without making social usefulness the measure of moral truth.
Prager's claim that an ethical realist must make pragmatic success decisive and that a godless moral system demonstrably fails.
After Prager equates realism with what works, Harris distinguishes the concepts and grounds objective ethical answers in degrees of possible happiness and suffering.
Claims that sacred books have supernatural authorship are divisive, dangerous, unsupported, and obstruct an effective response to religious extremism.
This identifies supernatural scriptural authority as the central harmful dogma and connects that thesis directly to moral and civilizational consequences.
After introductory material, Harris states the principal case against religious dogma and explains why he considers its social effects especially dangerous.
Religious Americans recognize Islamic totalitarianism more reliably than secular academics, contradicting the claim that religiosity impedes moral judgment.
The argument supplies Prager's principal empirical test of which worldview better identifies contemporary evil and directly challenges Harris's causal account.
Harris's claim that American religiosity obstructs an effective response to Islam and moral progress.
Prager distinguishes American religion from Islamist ideology and argues that religious conservatives, unlike secular institutions, perceive the principal contemporary threat.
Religious conservatives may recognize Islamist danger, but they do so because they understand how belief in divine books can rationally motivate violent conduct.
This preserves Harris's critique despite Prager's empirical counterexample by treating conservative recognition as evidence about the behavioral force of dogma.
Prager's argument that religious Americans' recognition of Islamist danger vindicates religious moral judgment.
Harris accepts the comparative observation but argues that religious believers recognize Islamist motives precisely because they understand sincere supernatural commitments.
The practical moral question is which worldview produces a better society, and secular institutions have failed to identify both communism and Islamic totalitarianism.
This reframes the dispute around demonstrated moral outcomes and states the core historical indictment supporting the divine-authority side of the motion.
Harris's insistence that beliefs must track factual reality and that unsupported religious explanations lack evidence.
Prager distinguishes whether religion is evidentially justified from whether religious or secular cultures are more capable of recognizing evil and making a good world.
Atheism did not cause communist or fascist atrocities; the operative cause was political dogma, and open-ended rational inquiry is the general remedy for unjustified belief.
The move answers the historical case against secularism while articulating Harris's general criterion for reliable moral and political reasoning.
Prager's claim that secular liberals failed against communism and Islam because their nonreligious worldview was morally defective.
Harris disputes the attribution of totalitarian evil to atheism and broadens his criticism from religious doctrine to every form of unjustified, closed dogma.
A creator and designer provide a more intellectually plausible explanation of existence than the view that persons and the world arose as sheer coincidence.
The argument supplies the metaphysical foundation for Prager's appeal to divine moral authority rather than relying only on its claimed social consequences.
Harris's contention that attributing moral rules to the creator is unjustified and unnecessary for discovering their wisdom.
The discussion shifts from comparative moral performance to justification, and Prager grounds his belief in God in creation, existence, and perceived design.
The Bible's exceptional moral character supports divine authorship, and apparently primitive rules can represent major moral advances in their historical setting.
This directly defends the epistemic and moral authority of sacred text against the charge that its violent or archaic provisions discredit divine origin.
Harris's challenge asking why anyone should regard the Bible as authored or informed by a supernatural deity.
Prager answers the challenge to biblical authority by appealing to the text's greatness and by interpreting a disputed legal principle as historical moral progress.
The prohibition on murder endures because it has divine authority, whereas grounding morality in human discussion places irrational confidence in human nature.
The move presents the clearest direct contrast between divine-command grounding and secular moral deliberation at the center of the stated motion.
Harris's claim that people can discover the wisdom of prohibiting murder through open-ended conversation without believing God commanded it.
After disputing scriptural penalties, Prager returns to moral foundations and argues that divine authority makes the murder prohibition more secure than human agreement.
Human cooperation, attachment, and the benefits of mutual care give societies practical grounds to reject murder without relying on divine commands.
This supplies an affirmative secular mechanism for moral convergence rather than merely criticizing scripture or denying the necessity of divine authority.
Prager's challenge that discussion with another person could validate murder and therefore cannot securely ground morality.
Harris responds to a counterexample about conversational morality by grounding anti-murder norms in cooperation, human psychology, social attachment, and viable coexistence.
Biblical law embodies a violently theocratic worldview comparable to modern religious tyranny, and subsequent moral progress required cultures to outgrow it.
The move challenges sacred texts as dependable moral guides by arguing that moral advancement occurred through departure from their theocratic prescriptions.
Prager's scholarly defense of biblical punishments and his claim that disputed ancient provisions can be rationally contextualized.
Following detailed disagreement over Sabbath punishment, Harris broadens the dispute from isolated passages to the overall political and moral character of biblical law.
